draft.description_short: Trump orders a second U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement

draft.description_long: On his first day back in office, January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order directing the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations to submit formal notice that the United States would withdraw from the Paris Agreement. It was the second time Trump had ordered a withdrawal: during his first term, the United States left the accord, and President Joe Biden later rejoined it in 2021. The 2025 order again reversed that policy and set a withdrawal process in motion; signing the order did not make the international withdrawal effective that same day. The Paris Agreement is the framework through which participating countries submit climate goals and report on efforts to limit warming. Leaving it reduces the United States’ participation in that shared process, although domestic emissions policy is also shaped by separate federal and state actions. This account focuses on the executive order and its diplomatic direction, rather than asserting unverified effects on other countries’ commitments or on U.S. emissions.

draft.title: Trump Issues Clemency Proclamation for January 6 Offenses
draft.description_short: On January 20, 2025, Trump issued a proclamation pardoning many people convicted of January 6 offenses, commuting named sentences and directing dismissal of pending indictments.
draft.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a clemency proclamation concerning offenses related to January 6, 2021. The proclamation granted pardons to certain defendants, commuted the sentences of named individuals, and directed the attorney general to dismiss pending indictments. It was not a Justice Department motion to vacate every conviction, and pardons or commutations are legally distinct from vacating convictions.
draft.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a presidential proclamation addressing federal offenses related to events at or near the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021. The proclamation granted pardons to certain people convicted of those offenses, commuted the sentences of specifically named individuals to time served, and directed the attorney general to dismiss pending indictments. These actions were executive clemency. They were not a Department of Justice motion asking a court to vacate all January 6 convictions, and the proclamation did not describe every conviction as vacated. The proclamation commuted the sentences of 14 named defendants, including Stewart Rhodes and Joseph Biggs, to time served; it pardoned all other people convicted of offenses related to January 6. It directed the Bureau of Prisons to release those held in prison immediately and ordered the attorney general to pursue dismissal with prejudice of pending indictments. Those terms distinguish this presidential clemency action from a court motion to vacate convictions.

draft.description_medium: In his August 20, 2026 New York Review of Books essay on Regime Change, Mark Danner describes Trump’s second-term governing style as a “constitutional dictatorship.” He links the argument to expansive executive power and emergency declarations, while noting that political and practical costs sometimes prompted retreats. The phrase is his interpretation, not a court finding or formal legal status.
draft.description_long: Mark Danner’s August 20, 2026 essay in the New York Review of Books reviews Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan’s book Regime Change and calls Trump’s second-term governing style a “constitutional dictatorship.” Danner argues that Trump expanded executive power by invoking emergencies and weakening Congress’s role, and uses the book’s reporting to discuss tariffs, immigration enforcement and other policies. He also notes occasions when Trump backed down after markets fell, courts intervened or political costs rose. The phrase is the essayist’s political characterization; it is not a court finding, legal status or description of one discrete order. The essay offers commentary on several actions and responses rather than a single event. The packet’s duplicate records carry different stored dates but cite this same NYRB essay, published on August 20. A publication-context summary should identify that essay and its argument without presenting Danner’s assessment as an established legal conclusion.
